item.title: NASA ends Swift space telescope mission after failed rescue attempt
item.description: null NASA has officially ended the mission of its Swift space telescope, after a private satellite failed in its bold bid to rescue the aging spacecraft. That rescue mission was led by the Arizona company Katalyst Space Technologies, whose LINK spacecraft tried to meet up with Swift this summer to boost its orbit. That didn't work out, however, so Swift continues its fall back toward Earth. The telescope is expected to reenter Earth's atmosphere "in the next few weeks," NASA said in a statement on Friday (Oct. 23). That statement served primarily to announce the end of the Swift mission after more than 20 very productive years. The telescope launched to Earth orbit in November 2004, tasked with studying gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) — the most powerful explosions in the cosmos. Swift was designed to operate for two years, but it continued studying the high-energy universe for more than two decades. "In that time, Swift played a major role in advancing our understanding of the changing universe and was part of a revolution in astrophysics that showed how critical rapid-response observations are to the entire community," Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director of the Astrophysics Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington, said in the statement. NASA had hoped to keep Swift going even longer. In September 2025, the agency awarded a contract to the Arizona company Katalyst Space Technologies to rescue the observatory, which was falling back to Earth thanks to atmospheric drag. Swift has no thrusters capable of counteracting this drag. So Katalyst built a refrigerator-sized spacecraft called LINK, which aimed to rendezvous with Swift, grapple it with three robotic arms and boost it to a higher orbit, allowing the observatory to continue its science work. NASA and Katalyst stressed from the start that success was far from guaranteed. After all, LINK's mission was unprecedented: No private spacecraft had ever captured and boosted a satellite that wasn't designed to be serviced in this way. And the rate of Swift's orbital decay demanded a rapid timeline: LINK launched on July 3 , a little over nine months after Katalyst won the $30 million NASA Swift-rescue contract. LINK was not able to execute its very challenging mission. About three weeks after liftoff, it suffered problems with its propulsion system and orientation-maintaining reaction wheels, which caused it to start spinning at an unexpected rate . These issues prevented LINK from capturing and boosting Swift, but the private craft did manage to get within 7.5 to 9.3 miles (12 to 15 kilometers) of the observatory and photograph it. "From the beginning, this was a high-risk, high-reward mission," Domagal-Goldman said in a statement on Sept. 25 , the day that LINK fell back to Earth. "And while we'll be sad to see Swift's mission come to a close, we knew this boost effort would be worthwhile either way — advancing U.S. spacecraft servicing technology, challenging us to meet unprecedented mission timelines, and

item.title: 'Donnie Darko' at 25: How a giant rabbit, time loops, and teen angst became a sci-fi cult classic
item.description: null "Have you ever seen a portal?" The term "cult classic" has been loosely bandied about in cinematic circles until its definition has diluted into nothingness, but never has it been more appropriately applied than to director Richard Kelly’s strange psychological sci-fi thriller, "Donnie Darko", which celebrates its milestone 25th birthday today. Starring Jake Gyllenhaal, Drew Barrymore, Mary McDonnell, Maggie Gyllenhaal, Patrick Swayze, Jena Malone, and Noah Wyle, "Donnie Darko" was released on Oct. 26, 2001, into an unstable world still shocked by the catastrophic Sept. 11 terrorist attacks less than two months earlier. The thrust of the narrative revolves around an alternative universe accidentally forming via a supernatural anomaly after a jet engine falls off a commercial airliner and crashes through the roof of a suburban Virginia home, landing in the bedroom of our troubled title character. As the frightening phantom of Frank the Bunny warns, this parallel reality has a ticking clock that’ll result in its imminent collapse in just 28 days, 6 hours, 42 minutes, and 12 seconds. From the haunting voice telling our heroic teen, "Wake up, Donnie," as the grandfather clock in the Darko residence ominously chimed midnight, to its exploration of the nature of mental illness, time travel paradoxes, fraudulent motivational speakers, teenage angst in the 1980s, and the logistics of interdimensional portals, "Donnie Darko" became an ideal parable for turbulent times. But Kelly's post-modern sci-fi fantasy emerged on the big screen when there existed a pervading fear of gathering in large groups as America was just beginning to recover and process the atrocities committed on 9/11. Newmarket Films was perplexed on precisely how to market the movie, as it is such a unique combination of genres that forges something far greater than the sum of its parts. Throughout that entire fall, "Donnie Darko" came and went in multiplexes with barely a whisper, pulling in just over $500K off of a meager $4.5 million budget. Years later, it would become a bona fide word-of-mouth sensation via several re-releases, home video editions, and further experiences in regularly sold-out midnight screenings on its way to earning cult status. "Donnie Darko" celebrates its 25th anniversary on Oct. 26, 2026. (Image credit: Newmarket Films) It's a deeply personal film that will affect any viewer who allows its meticulously slow build to seduce them into its dreamlike sphere. Much has been debated and discussed about its many metaphors and symbolism, which employed elements of a splintered universe long before the multiverse was hijacked by Hollywood superhero spectacles. It’s a raw meditation on death more than anything, and its labyrinth of quantum entanglements feeds our existential core. item.title: Microsoft releases emergency .NET security fixes for Google Brotli bug
item.description: To address a vulnerability in Google's Brotli compression technology that could allow attackers to corrupt process memory, Microsoft is urging .NET users to update "as soon as possible" after releasing an out-of-band (OOB) security update. It released new versions for .NET 8, 9, 10, and .NET 11 to patch against the Brotli bug, following similar updates from Node.js, Python, and other projects. Senior program manager Rahul Bhandari said in the October 25 release that the buffer overflow vulnerability in Brotli, tracked as CVE-2026-111497 and rated 8.1 under CVSS v3.1 in Microsoft's advisory, could allow an unauthenticated attacker to read or corrupt process memory, potentially resulting in information disclosure, denial of service, or elevation of privilege. Microsoft’s own advisory for the vulnerability, which some are referring to as Broccoli2Shell or Node2Shell, confirms that while experts have cobbled working exploits together , there is nothing to suggest that criminals are using them in successful attacks. However, its exploitability assessment reads: “Exploitation More Likely.” Broccoli2Shell was first disclosed on October 21 by the Node.js team, which released fixes for ten vulnerabilities, the most serious of which was CVE-2026-111497. Node.js credited Khai Tran and Sylvie Mayer of OpenAI’s Codex Security with the discovery, but failed to mention why it was only recognized as a security flaw and disclosed properly in October, despite the underlying bug having been fixed in Brotli's source code in February. OpenAI filled in the gap with a Xeet : “This root cause issue was actually fixed in the Brotli source code in February, but it wasn’t known at the time that it gave rise to a security vulnerability, and there was no more recent release of Brotli. “Since Brotli is built into other software, any software which includes this library needs to take the update too, followed by the users of that software.” Attackers can exploit vulnerable systems by providing them with malicious Brotli-compressed data via a specially crafted request. The vulnerability went slightly under the radar due to the disclosure timing closely aligning with that of PHP2Shell , although fixing the critical flaw should be a priority due to the range of technologies that are affected. In addition to .NET, Node.js, and Python, Bun , Envoy , and Istio have all released patches, and JFrog has worked up an exploit affecting FFmpeg using a specially crafted JPEG XL image, extending the exploit path beyond HTTP. It said that FFmpeg reaches Brotli through libjxl, which it uses to decompress metadata stored in brob boxes within the image format. The same researchers said the vulnerability affects Apache Arrow too, with attackers able to cause a denial of service. Merav Bar, threat researcher at Wiz, added that cloud users are exposed extensively, noting that 91 percent of cloud environments rely on components vulnerable to the Brotli flaw and that 82 percent of cloud environments

item.title: Highway thieves are spoofing GPS to steal millions in data center-bound cargo
item.description: Highway thieves are using sophisticated digital tactics that investigators worry make it easy to rob trucks carrying millions in expensive data center equipment. NBC News spoke to “several industry leaders, consultants, and investigators advising law enforcement” offices probing the biggest thefts yet and reported that since June, thieves have “made away with more than $100 million in data center freight.” Here’s how they said thieves get away with it: First, thieves hack freight brokers’ accounts on shipment-listing websites and post fake shipments to lure real bids, then send a malicious link to any trucking companies that respond. Once victims click, thieves install software to take control of their accounts and start bidding on real shipments. Sometimes, a real delivery driver is hired to collect the cargo, unaware of the scam, and other times fake driver’s licenses are used to get accomplices hired. Either way, the goods are eventually transferred to a driver working with the thieves to resell the gear, and, in one of the largest thefts, tracking coordinates were spoofed to prevent digital monitoring. item.title: Open source keyboard lets you swap parts like magnetic Lego bricks
item.description: The world is full of different keyboard layouts, but if you want one that's completely customized, down to the individual key, there's a new open source project that uses magnets to hold interchangeable pieces together. Keybytes is an open source project that allows any ambitious builder to create a fully modular keyboard - and we’re talking FULLY modular here. Each key contains its own RISC-V microcontroller and pogo pins on all four sides, providing power and I2C connections between adjacent modules so users can rearrange the keys into different layouts. The only extra component needed is a controller module, which coordinates the individual keys and handles communication with the host computer. And good news: Despite consisting of two stacked circuit boards, it has the same footprint as the single-key modules that attach to it. The entire thing was designed by a Massachusetts Institute of Technology freshman named Nathan Alspaugh, who is studying aerospace engineering. Alspaugh has always wanted to design his own keyboard, and who better than an MIT student to go over the top in building the most intricate, overengineered version imaginable? “I had always wanted to make a keyboard but I didn't want to be locked into just one design so I wanna make it so that I can rearrange it at any time,” Alspaugh said in the first entry of his project journal , which he’s been keeping since March of this year. “I searched online and couldn't find it anywhere so I decided to make it myself.” The main readme in the GitHub project isn’t super detailed, instead mostly describing what the project entails for anyone willing to give it a shot (custom printed circuit boards, Cherry MX switches, 3D-printed cases, and a whole lot of tiny soldered components). It’s Alspaugh’s journal where the depth of the work he did is laid bare for all to see, and boy did he do a lot of work. Designing a single-key modular keyboard from scratch is no easy task, and the journal details a number of setbacks that Alspaugh faced, like magnets that wouldn’t stay put, design compromises, and - of course - plenty of board errors that he luckily was able to catch in the design phase before spending a bunch of cash ordering custom components. Alspaugh also had to learn to use a resin 3D printer for the project, and of course multiple iterations and a bunch of manual modifications had to be made to get everything to properly fit together. Alspaugh told The Register he’s spent around 100 hours on the project so far. And then there’s the cost: All those tiny custom boards don’t come cheap. According to a shopping cart for the board designs included in his journal, the Keybits (the individual key control boards) cost only a couple of bucks apiece, but the Keywords (controller boards) cost $30 a pop. Alspaugh opted to have the manufacturer fully assemble the boards, which is where a good deal of the cost came from: Keybit assembly cost him $69, while Keyword assembly cost him $203. Alspaugh said

item.title: Reddit's r/opensource bans AI slop, and quite a few humans for good measure
item.description: Reddit's r/opensource community has declared war on AI-generated software by introducing a sweeping set of new rules that also manage to shut out solo developers, newcomers, and anyone who doesn't speak English. The crackdown , announced over the weekend, bans projects that use AI, that were created with AI, or that are intended for AI applications. "The long story short, if your project uses AI, is made by AI, or is intended for AI, it's not welcome on r/opensource," moderator Wolvereness wrote. "AI, as it exists today, is incongruent to this Open Source community." To get a project featured on the subreddit, developers now need to show it has been actively maintained for at least a year, has an established community, and has at least three contributors, give or take. Student projects such as note-taking apps and PDF viewers aren't welcome either, and developers can no longer use the subreddit to find people willing to help maintain their software. That creates a chicken-and-egg problem for independent developers, who apparently need an established community before they can use an open source forum to find one. Even projects with no AI involvement could fall foul of the rules. One Reddit user pointed out that their nine-year-old project, which has more than 300 GitHub stars and dozens of resolved issues, would no longer qualify because they're its sole contributor. The moderator also imposed a minimum Reddit account age of one year and requires significant prior contributions. Anyone who attempts to post and then contacts the moderators seeking an exception risks being permanently banned and muted. Perhaps the most eyebrow-raising restriction concerns language. "If you don't speak English, you need to find a different community," the announcement states. Moderators say they cannot distinguish AI-written content from AI-translated text, and that non-English speakers cannot verify whether a translation is accurate. That particular rule has gone down about as well as you might expect. Fellow moderator ssddanbrown publicly objected, saying they hadn't been consulted about the changes and only learned of them through moderation notifications. "I don't agree with that rule. Especially so with how it was said," they wrote. The rules also raise awkward questions about projects like Linux, whose developers have taken a different approach to AI-assisted contributions. The kernel allows developers to use the technology while holding them responsible for the resulting code. Earlier this month, maintainers even decided to drop the requirement to disclose AI assistance . Asked whether that meant Linux would be banned from r/opensource, Wolvereness suggested it would probably still be allowed, arguing that enforcement would depend on whether a project was obviously the product of AI-generated code. "There's no 'objective' way to implement this policy," the moderator acknowledged. Apparently, AI is forbidden unless the moderators decide otherwise. The row comes

item.title: Record breaker! Astronomers spot powerful cosmic explosion that lasted 27 days
item.description: null Astronomers have spotted a remarkable gamma-ray burst (GRB) that's a real Incredible Hulk compared to other cosmic explosions of the same type. What makes this GRB so special is the fact that the central engine powering it remained active for around 27 days, flaring in X-rays following the initial blast. That's 20 days longer than the longest previous GRB on record. This record-breaking burst — which is designated GRB 220706A and was spotted on July 6, 2022 — is even more exciting because scientists don't know what the central engine powering it actually is. "In a nutshell, GRB 220706A is an extremely late X-ray flare. X-ray flaring is common following GRBs, but previously it has always come within the first few days after we detect the burst," study team member Benjamin Gompertz, of the University of Birmingham in England, told Space.com. "The fact that we see flaring at around 27 days in the GRB’s rest frame tells us that there’s an ongoing active process, and that’s unprecedented in the known population," Gompertz added. "The previous record for delayed flaring was about six days after the GRB." What created the Incredible Hulk of gamma-ray bursts? GRBs are some of the most powerful explosions in the cosmos. They have been linked to the collapse of a massive star, which also triggers a supernova and creates a black hole . This results in a long-duration GRB, while short-duration GRBs are thought to be triggered when two stellar remnants called neutron stars collide. GRB 220706A is an example of an ultra-long GRB, a rare cosmic blast of gamma rays in which the engine powering the GRB stays active for longer. They are incredibly rare, with their cause still unknown. "We don’t know what the central engine driving this outburst is, and that’s what makes this such a compelling event," Gompertz said. "The fact that we see a supernova tells us that a star has collapsed, which is the standard power source for GRBs, but it doesn’t immediately account for the extremely late flaring or unusually bright supernova. We can interpret that through previous events to some degree." Gompertz added that another ultra-long GRB detected in 2011, GRB 111209A , was associated with an unusually bright supernova (SN2011k) that had clear evidence for a central engine. The team behind that research determined that GRB 111209A is powered by a magnetar, a neutron star with a particular powerful magnetic field. In this case, the magnetic field is rotating at around 1,000 times per second. "Our supernova looks a lot like that one, so a magnetar might be present here. That ties in nicely with super-luminous supernovas, which are also thought to be magnetar-driven," Gompertz said. "Another possibility could be that the GRB jet and the supernova are colliding with shells of dense material that were ejected towards the end of the parent star’s life, as it became unstable and began ejecting its outer layers. This sort of event is also seen in the super-luminous supernova pop

item.title: UK pentester 'killa' claims $2K Bitcoin prize in PHP2Shell capture-the-flag contest
item.description: A UK-based developer and pentester has claimed a $2,000 Bitcoin prize for demonstrating the exploitability of the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities that melted the internet last week. Jaydip Modhwadia, 26, otherwise known as “Killa,” claimed the prize set by James Pavur, who launched the "Steal My Bitcoin" site on October 24. Pavur launched the CTF (capture the flag) challenge to prove that the PHP2Shell exploit was not as easy as those in the cybersecurity community claimed it to be, promising to award $2,000 in Bitcoin to anyone who could achieve Remote Code Execution (RCE) on his website. "My Bitcoin was stolen after 19.28 hours," the website now says, after Modhwadia claimed the prize, although the real time taken is thought to be less than three hours. Soon after Pavur launched the CTF on Saturday, prospective flag-catchers complained that the website he set up, which served only static HTML, was not built in a way that allowed the PHP2Shell exploit to achieve RCE. The web page was running a vulnerable version of PHP, but the exploit path required a vulnerable website to serve a PHP file for flag-catchers to use as a hook – something that Pavur seemingly updated at around 1300 UTC on October 25. Modhwadia achieved RCE on the website, exposing a PHP endpoint, at 1547 UTC. After an error from Pavur placing the wrong wallet key on the server, the CTF creator sent Modhwadia his award, which the community upped to $2,000 from Pavur’s initial $500. The pentester published a write-up of his method, a single-file Python script he says requires 20 HTTP requests "at most" to fully execute. Speaking to The Register , Modhwadia also confirmed that he got the flag in "around three or so hours in total." He said he followed the news about the competition, "but didn't attempt it until it gained significant notice." If he had attempted it before Pavur introduced the endpoint, he may have struggled. For hours, bug bounty hunters were trying to access the website to attempt the challenge, as news of the CTF had exploded across tech circles. "The fact that it took 19 hours was because after it went popular, the entire site became basically unusable for anyone at all," Modhwadia added. The challenge saw a huge number of attempts, despite Pavur's decision to introduce a prohibitive 1MB request limit on Nginx. Alon Gal, co-founder and CTO at Hudson Rock, commended Modhwadia's work, but added that his success achieved in just a few hours should not be taken to mean that the same attack could be automated at scale. He said : "Does this mean autonomous AI agents can now compromise arbitrary PHP servers at scale? No. This was a sophisticated, target-specific exploit. "But it does demonstrate that PHP2Shell can be weaponized against a live target, even with meaningful technical constraints." Modhwadia's proof of concept is not the first to prove PHP2Shell is exploitable, but it falls under the more advanced category. Early signs suggested that Address Space Layout Randomizati

item.title: Predatory amphibians swam the seas 237 million years ago
item.description: Gerrothorax maritimus , a fully marine amphibian from the Late Triassic Period Ryosuke Motani/UC Davis The Late Triassic seas contained a multitude of marine reptiles, but lurking on the sea floor was something different: a marine amphibian. A fossil of the large, bottom-dwelling ambush predator discovered in China is the first evidence that amphibians once found a way to adapt to life in the ocean. Named Gerrothorax maritimus , the near-perfect and exquisitely preserved 74-centimetre-long fossil was found by farmers in what is now a national geopark in Guanling county, China. The researchers who studied the fossil think that its secret to survival in salt water, which is normally fatal to amphibians because of their permeable skin, probably lay in its strong body armour. Advertisement Read more Stunning early mammal fossil sheds light on the evolution of suckling “It was a flat animal that lived on the sea floor,” says Ryosuke Motani at the University of California, Davis, who was part of the team that analysed the fossil. It was probably an ambush feeder, he says, as its wide mouth and the strong hyoid bone in its neck suggest it used suction feeding, as is seen in some modern bottom-dwelling predators of a similar size that use an ambush strategy, such as wobbegong sharks. As soon as the researchers began to study the fossil, they knew it was neither fish nor reptile. It had to be an early amphibian because of its tell-tale anatomy, which included its four legs and gills. There is, however, no evidence that the creature underwent metamorphosis, as many modern amphibians do, such as when tadpoles become frogs, says Motani. Subscriber-only newsletter Sign up to Editor’s Highlights Sign up to newsletter To prove that the animal was indeed marine and not just a land-based creature washed into the sea after death, the researchers studied the strontium isotope ratios of the fossil bones. They found that the remains of the new species had a clear signature of sea water, meaning G. maritimus grew to adulthood while in the ocean. Palaeogeographic reconstructions also suggest that, 237 million years ago in the Late Triassic Period, the location in which the fossil was discovered was at least 30 kilometres away from land. The fossil was also recovered alongside that of a large marine reptile: an ichthyosaur called Guizhouichthyosaurus , which reached lengths of 7 metres. Read more Fossil mammal with reptile-like teeth changes picture of our evolution Interestingly, the closest relative to G. maritimus lived in freshwater environments. A fossil of this amphibian, Gerrothorax pulcherrimus , was first described nearly a century ago. This has led the researchers to suggest the marine lifestyle of G. maritimus was an accident of evolution. “There was a freshwater amphibian that happened to have the equipment needed to colonise the sea – the body armour,” says Motani. The armour originally protected the Gerrothorax genus from predators in fresh water. But beca

item.title: SpaceX ignites giant Super Heavy booster engines ahead of daring Starship launch (video)
item.description: null SpaceX is shooting for new heights with its upcoming Starship test flight, and the booster tapped for the mission is in its final stretch of preparations before the mission. The Super Heavy booster for Flight Test 15, Booster 22, underwent a static test fire on Sunday (Oct. 25), igniting all of its Raptor 3 engines for about 15 seconds. "Full duration 33-engine static fire for the Super Heavy booster preparing for Flight 15," SpaceX said in a post on X . The test is a beginning of final checks on the first-stage vehicle, which will be mated with the Flight 15 upper stage, Ship 42, ahead of launch, but not before the spacecraft completes some tests of its own. SpaceX conducts a static-fire test with the Flight 15 Starship Super Heavy B22 at its Starbase site in South Texas on Oct. 25, 2026. (Image credit: SpaceX) Ship 42 will also complete a series of tests as the next Starship launch approaches, including a static engine fire and final systems checks. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has stated that SpaceX will attempt the first launch tower catch of a ship upper stage on Flight 15, which, if successful, would be a significant step forward for the company's goal to mature Starship to full reusability. SpaceX's confidence in its ability to catch both the Super Heavy and Ship stages has been building this year, following three launches so far in 2026. Its most recent (Sept. 28) mission, Flight 14, reached orbit for the first time and performed the successful deployment of 26 next-generation Starlink V3 satellites, marking the first operational payloads delivered to orbit by the spacecraft. Starlink V3 satellites are too big to fit aboard the company's workhorse Falcon 9 rocket. Flight 14 wasn't without setbacks, however. An upper-stage Raptor engine shut down prematurely during ascent, prompting SpaceX to cut the planned 10-hour mission short. Ship, nevertheless, completed a controlled reentry and splashed down in the Pacific Ocean about three hours after liftoff. Flight 15 could carry another batch of V3 Starlinks, though SpaceX has not officially confirmed a payload. Beginning to upgrade its global network with the fast V3 satellites, however, is a major reason SpaceX is pushing to bring Starship into regular service. Full duration 33-engine static fire for the Super Heavy booster preparing for Flight 15 https://t.co/7eqbC4h0Fh October 25, 2026 Starship's development also has implications for NASA's Artemis program, which has contracted SpaceX to develop a modified Ship upper stage capable of landing astronauts on the surface of the moon. NASA recently updated the timeline of milestones SpaceX needs to accomplish with Starship before a lunar lander version will qualify to carry crews, with a significant demonstration mission coming up next summer on Artemis III. item.title: Trumpets blare and skies part as AI hypefest culminates in Anthropic IPO filing
item.description: Anthropic has filed for an IPO that could rank among Wall Street's biggest ever, revealing an $80.7 billion half-year loss, a startlingly complex governance structure, and warnings that its AI models could blackmail humans, resist shutdown, or create "existential risks" to society. The Claude maker filed its S-1 registration statement with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday as it prepares to list on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT. The company has not yet disclosed its proposed share price or how many shares it plans to sell. Of the filing's 614 pages, 94 are devoted to risk factors. But it's Anthropic's financial figures that are likely to raise eyebrows first. The Claude maker reported $16.3 billion in revenue for the first six months of 2026, up from $1.2 billion a year earlier. It also posted a whopping $80.7 billion net loss, although $72.4 billion of that was an accounting adjustment tied to the company's soaring valuation, not money it actually spent. Anthropic's operating loss was considerably smaller at $693 million, down from $2.1 billion a year earlier. By its own adjusted accounting, the company made a $1.6 billion operating profit in the first half of 2026, for a margin of around 10 percent. Whether it can keep making money on those terms is another matter. Training and running Claude requires an eye-watering amount of computing power, and Anthropic will need much more to keep pace with its rivals. A $1.6 billion adjusted profit won't count for much if the infrastructure bills keep growing faster than the business. Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, told The Register that Anthropic's IPO could leave ordinary investors paying a premium for growth that has yet to translate into sustained profits. "A huge pool of private capital has allowed AI businesses to scale up and command extraordinary valuations long before they reach the stock market," she said, adding that investors buying in at the IPO will face a price with "a hefty dose of future success baked in." The financial risks are fairly conventional by Silicon Valley standards, but the warnings about what Claude might get up to are perhaps less so. Anthropic claims that models, including its own, have exhibited unexpected or self-preserving behavior, including attempts to resist shutdown, conceal information, and produce outputs resembling blackmail. It also warns that sufficiently advanced AI systems could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to society” if deployed without adequate safeguards. That's not to say Claude is currently blackmailing customers. Anthropic has observed some of this behavior in testing, but it also identifies more immediate security concerns as it gives its models access to external tools, code repositories, and corporate systems. Anthropic warns that attackers could hide malicious instructions in websites, documents, or API responses that its AI agents can access. If an agent follows those instructions, it could

item.title: Daniel Etim Effiong Battles M.I Abaga in a fierce Cook-off at the Premiere of Cooking with GameChangers’ Season 2
item.description: Pressure mounted daily as a one-week cook-off countdown marked the premiere of Season 2 of Cooking With GameChangers . Cooking with GameChangers is a business-reality and cooking competition show where business executives are filmed through a day in their life and thereafter engage in a cook-off to make the best meal, which would be tasted by the show judges, and an “Ultimate GameChanger” is announced. Season 1 of the show aired in 2024 and garnered over 60 million TV viewers in a quarter. Season 2 of Cooking with GameChangers premiered with a week-long cook-off that saw corporate leaders and media icons trade their laptops and workspaces for aprons and kitchen workstations in a dramatic twist. The cook-off week hosted by social media sensation, Steve Chuks , reached a crescendo on Friday, October 23rd, 2026, with a live-streamed event that featured an entertaining cook-off between the show host, Daniel Etim Effiong , and one of the show judges, M.I Abaga . People that followed live updates on Instagram @cookingwithgamechangers got to experience the unforgettable moments delivered all through the daily live cook-offs between industry giants. The live cook-offs can be watched here . The live cook-off spotlighted organisations that lead in their respective sectors, hence serving as a pat-on-the-back for the great work being done to stay at the top. This cook-off, however, pushed our corporate contestants to their limit as they battled against the ticking clock to present their best interpretation of the assigned dish of yam and egg with peppered sauce. The panel of judges also brought their unique perspectives from business, entertainment, food, culture and leadership, holding back nothing as they tasted, critiqued and delivered sharp, witty feedback before the winner got announced. The show’s executive producer, Seyi Banigbe , joined the panel of judges from Monday to Wednesday as she kept the contestants on their feet even as she bridged humour with her culinary grit while delivering a detailed analysis of each contestant’s cooking effort. Day 1 kicked off on Monday, 19th October, with a cook-off between companies leading in the ethnic radio broadcast industry. The battle was between Wazobia FM, represented by Ogar Justina , and Naija FM, represented by Godwin Aruwayo . Both contestants did their best to deliver a great variation of yam and egg with pepper sauce, but Naija FM emerged the winner. Day 1 of the premiere cook-off started with so much excitement and fun. Day 2 featured News TV giants with New Central Television and TVC News represented. The fierce standoff between the two contestants was palpable as they brought their professional mien to the kitchen. TVC News was represented by their head of news, Babajide Kolade-Otitoju , and News Central’s head of programmes, Tolulope Adeleru-Balogun , the two bantered and shared highlights on their careers and respective news stations. item.title: Family Business Summit 2026: Calls for Stronger Succession Planning and Governance to Secure Generational Legacy
item.description: The Family Business Summit 2026 has concluded in Lagos with a call for Nigerian family businesses to strengthen governance, embrace succession planning and invest in next-generation leadership to build enterprises that endure beyond their founders. Held from October 15 to 17 under the theme “ Beyond the Founder: Scaling Family Businesses Across Generations ,” the summit convened business leaders, entrepreneurs, investors, wealth management experts and family enterprise advisers for three days of discussions on business continuity, wealth preservation and sustainable growth. Organised by My Family, My Business, in partnership with BusinessDay and PwC , the summit featured keynote addresses, panel sessions, masterclasses, a Deal Room, a succession workshop and the Family Business Leadership Awards 2026 as discussions explored succession planning, family governance, investment strategies, global wealth structuring, women’s leadership, technology and international expansion. In his welcome address, Oghenevwoke Ighure, Convener of the summit, emphasised the need for family businesses to move beyond founder-dependent structures and establish institutions capable of surviving across generations. “ The success of this year’s summit reinforces our belief that family businesses need more than the determination of their founders to endure; they need the right structures, values and leadership to thrive across generations. Our goal is to create a platform where families can have honest conversations, learn from one another’s experiences and access the knowledge and networks required to build sustainable institutions. Ultimately, succession is not just about transferring ownership; it is about preparing the next generation to lead, preserve the family legacy and create even greater value for the future .” Frank Aigbogun , Publisher of BusinessDay, Sam Abu , Country Senior Partner, PwC Nigeria and Regional Senior Partner, West Market, and Bolaji Balogun, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Chapel Hill Denham delivered keynote addresses, while Esiri Agbeyi , PwC Nigeria Partner and Africa Family Business Leader, presented findings from the PwC Africa Family Business Survey. Bolaji Balogun , Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Chapel Hill Denham, addressed the role of patient capital in building businesses that endure. “ Building a family business that endures across generations requires more than reinvesting capital; it demands a clear distinction between family wealth and corporate resources, strong governance, integrity and a relentless commitment to excellence ,” Balogun said, stressing the importance of capital markets, long-term financing and developing the competence and character of future generations. Sam Abu , Country Senior Partner, PwC Nigeria speaking on the importance of succession planning in family businesses, said: “ Inheritance is not the same as succession. item.title: Last call for The Register’s data sovereignty dinner in Washington
item.description: This Thursday, 29 October, The Register hosts HPE and NVIDIA at one dinner table in Washington to answer the question that stalls AI in regulated industries: where the data lives, who can reach it, and what an auditor will accept as evidence a year from now. The table is nearly set. If you have been meaning to ask for a place, this is the week. Editor-in-chief Matt Rosoff chairs. HPE sends Bharath Ramesh, Head of Product, AI Factory Solutions, and Tracy Mills, Acting Director Federal Systems Integrators and Distinguished Chief Technologist Federal. NVIDIA sends Bert Condensa, Vice President for Enterprise AI Factory Segment Sales. They are there to take questions, with no slides and no recording, and the chair stops a pitch before it starts. The evening runs under the Chatham House Rule. That is the point of it. The things worth knowing about sovereign AI infrastructure, such as what a bank had to rebuild or which option somebody paid for and would not buy again, get said at a table like this and nowhere else. The agenda: which infrastructure options hold a boundary, what each one costs, and whether any of it survives production. The seats are for technology, data and risk leaders in healthcare, financial services, research, pharmaceuticals, government and higher education. Dinner runs from 6.00pm to 8.30pm at Fiola Mare, Washington DC. Places go by invitation and the last of them are going now. Request one here . Government and public sector guests: where your agency’s ethics rules require it, you can pay your own share and we will provide a receipt. Please say so when you request an invitation.

item.title: F1 in Texas: The American race that fans love to attend
item.description: Audi provided flights from Washington, DC, to Austin, Texas, and accommodation so Ars could attend the US Grand Prix. Ars does not accept paid editorial content. AUSTIN, Texas—Formula 1 returned to US shores this weekend with its annual visit to the Circuit of the Americas in Austin, Texas. Once in danger of falling off the calendar due to lack of interest, it’s now one of the most popular tracks on the calendar and, of the US’s three races, it's the one the real fans mostly attend. Unlike Miami or Las Vegas, which race on temporary street circuits, COTA is a permanent race track with plenty of run-off areas instead of concrete walls. Designed by motorcycle racer Kevin Schwanz—Herman Tilke’s company did only the buildings and infrastructure, contrary to popular belief—the track combines a mix of corner speeds with challenging turn sequences, a few heavy braking zones, and plenty of elevation changes. It’s a place Ars knows rather intimately by now. We’ve driven it in everything from an Audi TT-S to a Corvette ZR1 to a bicycle , and that’s just in the real world . Over the years, we’ve been there for F1 to learn about how the sport puts together its broadcasts , how Pirelli designs its tires , and how various tech partners help teams manage their data and strategies. We even saw the race through a neophyte’s eyes . And that’s just F1—we’ve logged many hours there with the World Endurance Championship and IMSA for the Lone Star Le Mans races in sweaty September . item.title: Swift operations end: 2004 spacecraft headed for fiery reentry
item.description: NASA's Swift observatory made its final observation on October 20 and is expected to re-enter the atmosphere in the next few weeks after a failed rescue attempt over the summer. Designed to study gamma-ray bursts, Swift was launched on November 20, 2004, on a two-year mission. It has lasted almost 22 years, but atmospheric drag is inexorably lowering the spacecraft's orbit, so reentry is likely just shy of the vehicle's 22nd anniversary. Swift has no propulsion system to save itself. Swift is now orbiting at an altitude of less than 171 miles above Earth's surface, meaning it cannot keep its telescopes steady when pointing at astronomical targets. Because the spacecraft could no longer compensate for the increased drag, it dropped into safe mode. A command was then sent from the ground that, according to NASA, "effectively ended Swift operations to prepare it for re-entry." The descent of Swift has accelerated in recent years due to increased solar activity. Last year, NASA awarded Katalyst Space a contract for a high-risk, high-reward mission to boost the observatory to a higher orbit. Swift's science operations were curtailed to maximize opportunities for Katalyst Space's LINK spacecraft, but alas, a rendezvous never happened , and engineers opted to reactivate operations to eke out as much science as possible. The expected side effect was increased drag on the spacecraft and, as expected, Swift sank rapidly until operations had to cease. Swift has been an astonishingly productive instrument during its long life. According to NASA, it has observed more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts and more than 1,400 supernova explosions. It has conducted an all-sky X-ray survey and seen stars shredded by black holes. The full Swift archive comes to approximately 12 terabytes. Not too bad for something that was only supposed to last two years. NASA now faces the problem that it has no direct replacement for Swift. As well as paying tribute to the observatory's contributions, Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director of the Astrophysics Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington, said in a statement: "To support rapid response to cosmic events in a post-Swift world, we're exploring our ability to use and augment NASA's fleet of existing space telescopes, from fast-to-orbit commercial capabilities to efficient, innovative new missions." ®

item.title: Glowing 'cauldron' of new stars | Space photo of the day for Oct. 26, 2026
item.description: null The James Webb Space Telescope's stunning view of the emission nebula N159 in the Large Magellanic Cloud. (Image credit: ESA/Webb, NASA & CSA, E. Sabbi, M. Zamani (ESA/Webb)Acknowledgement: M. H. Özsaraç) The NASA/ESA James Webb Space Telescope has captured a breathtaking view of a majestic star-forming region shining 161,000 light-years from Earth in a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way known as the Large Magellanic Cloud. What is it? The deep-space image reveals a 230-light-year-wide swathe of the glowing emission nebula N159, threaded with denser filaments of reddish molecular hydrogen that hide countless energetic young stars . Ghostly blue clouds of ionized hydrogen gas (H II) glow in the center of the image, having been energized by the ultraviolet radiation pouring out from nearby stars, whose winds helped create the chaotic structure of the vast stellar nursery. The ethereal pockets are surrounded by roiling orange clouds of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons — a type of organic molecule that may account for 30% of all carbon in the universe, according to the U.S. Department of Energy . Why is it incredible? N159 is estimated to be less than 3 million years old, making it one of the youngest star-forming regions in the Large Magellanic Cloud. It also has a markedly different composition than the stellar nurseries that spawn stars in our Milky Way , boasting a lower metal content that could mirror environments that existed in the early universe. By pointing JWST at N159, astronomers open a window to the distant past. They can compare the characteristics of stars at varying stages of evolution, including pre-main-sequence stars that are still in the process of forming, or accreting from the vast interstellar cloud. Want to know more? Be sure to check out our JWST explainer page to discover everything that you need to know about the space telescope, and peruse our astronomy coverage for the latest discoveries made possible by its 21.3-foot-wide (6.5-meter) golden eye.

item.title: Private equity giant: AI payoff strictly limited to Big Tech
item.description: AI has yet to deliver any financial payoff to US businesses outside of the tech sector, according to investment biz Apollo Global Management. The global asset firm made the claim in a posting to its Daily Spark blog that features analysis on the US economy and capital markets. It says corporate America is starting to view token spending not as a source of growth, but rather as a cost center that weighs on company margins. Apollo’s chief economist Torsten Slok says that revenue per worker may be rising for the so-called "Magnificent Seven" tech firms, which includes the hyperscalers plus Apple, Nvidia and Tesla, but this isn't the case for the rest of the S&P 500 businesses. The same goes for profit margins, and for AI boosting corporate productivity growth, he adds, posting charts to back up these claims. Apollo's assertion has met with pushback from some, who commented on social media that they did not recognize the picture painted by Slok. Others said a similar effect was noted in the PC industry, when productivity growth lagged the widespread adoption of computers in business by a decade or more. However the investment firm’s observations chime with various reports The Register has analyzed over the past year or two, such as one earlier this year from PwC that found the majority of chief executives had enjoyed neither increased revenue nor decreased costs from AI, despite investing heavily in the technology. Research from professional services firm Deloitte also showed that adopting AI tools has not helped the bottom line for most companies, while a separate report found AI is now facing corporate accountability after several years of investment with little or no return, and projects will have to prove their worth or be axed. McKinsey reckons the corporate world is now at a turning point and on the road to seeing a return for all the effort that organizations have put into pilots and early AI deployments – although it concedes the number of businesses reporting an actual earnings boost from their AI initiatives has remained flat. Slok questions whether mainstream corporations will ever be able to turn AI projects into higher revenue growth and higher profit margins, despite the appearance of cheaper or open-sourced models. In business, intelligence is mostly judgment, he says, and therefore depends on context. He notes that AI does not really understand anything, but especially accountability, trust, culture, unwritten rules, ethical trade-offs or fairness, all of which shape companies' reputational risk and ultimately drive revenue growth and profit margins. Apollo also notes a slowdown in token spending growth , claiming this shows the spending is highly price-sensitive and demand falls away or switches to cheap open source alternatives in response to even modest increases in cost. This casts doubt over the economics of pouring billions into constructing ever more datacenters if the resulting compute is only likely to turn a marginal profit.

item.title: We shouldn't be surprised about the PHPocalypse, as the internet is built on sticks and glue
item.description: We've spent the past several decades using duct tape, string, and chewing gum to chain the world's computers together into this thing we call the internet, so there's really no good reason to be surprised that most of it is full of software containing vulnerabilities that are practically just as old. You can listen to the latest episode of The Kettle right here on this page, as well as on Spotify , Apple Music, or YouTube . Those platforms also let you subscribe to Kettle, so you are always notified when the latest episode goes live. The world is still reeling from the PHP2Shell revelations that hit the news cycle this week, and on The Kettle there's no better topic for host Brandon Vigliarolo , cybersecurity editor Jessica Lyons , and FOSS reporter Liam Proven to tease apart. Join us to discuss what exactly is going on, how AI was key to finding another issue no human likely ever would have discovered on their own, and why exposing more bad code in the backbone of the world's computers might be just what we need to rethink the whole thing for the better. A lightly edited transcript follows: Brandon (00:01) Hi everyone, and welcome to the latest episode of The Register 's Kettle podcast. I'm your host, Reg reporter Brandon Vigliarolo. And hey, there's only one thing we could focus on for this week's episode, given all the hubbub around it, and that's the PHP apocalypse. It turns out most of the internet is running software that could allow remote code execution on host systems via a pair, or as of today apparently three, vulnerabilities that have come to collectively be known as PHP2Shell . So that's not great. With me to talk about this is our security editor Jessica Lyons and open source reporter Liam Proven, who has a few things to say about PHP itself and why it's probably not surprising we're finding ourselves in this mess. Thanks to you both for coming on. Liam Proven (00:43) Absolute pleasure. Jessica Lyons (00:43) Nice to be here. Brandon (00:44) So Jess, let's start with the basics. What is this? How big of a problem is it? And where do we stand on getting things fixed? Jessica Lyons (00:51) Great. The short answer is it's a very big problem. So we have these two related memory safety vulnerabilities, and they are in the PHP core. Collectively they're called PHP2Shell, and they affect every version that's been released in the last decade affected by one or both of these, going back to about version 5.4. So the general consensus is this is about 70 percent of all of the websites on the internet are running this code. So it basically affects everyone at this point. What happened here is that this dates actually back to August. An independent researcher first spotted this, and then we can talk a little bit more later about who found more of the exploits and what the (PHP) Foundation did with that. item.title: UK Biobank back online soon, months after someone tried to sell 500k people's data on Alibaba
item.description: UK Biobank (UKB) says its platform is now "secure" and that academics will soon regain access, months after a major data leak of volunteer health data. The charity, which runs the eponymous research project and describes itself as the custodian of the world's most comprehensive biomedical dataset, said it is waiting for approval from health data controllers and central government before it relaunches the platform. UK Biobank's Research Analysis Platform (UKB-RAP) has locked out all medical researchers trying to access its dataset since the April attack , which led to all 500,000 volunteers’ data being listed for sale on Chinese ecommerce website Alibaba. More than 20,000 researchers use the dataset provided by the cloud-based platform. They upload research projects and run experiments informed by the genomic data UKB collected from 40-to-69-year-olds between 2006 and 2010. The org makes around 30 petabytes worth of the stuff available to researchers, who investigate conditions including cancer, dementia, Parkinson’s disease, and COVID-19 immunity. Professor Sir Rory Collins, CEO at UKB, said on Friday that the organization has "completed the work to ensure that the UKB-RAP is secure," and that the progress was checked by an independent cybersecurity company, whose report recommends reopening the platform. The charity will begin a phased re-introduction of researchers to its platform after it receives the necessary approvals, although boffins will not be able to download any results files at first. The platform will pilot a "manual output checking system," where human reviewers will inspect files researchers wish to download before allowing them to do so, ahead of an automated process expected to roll out next year. According to the guide UKB compiled for researchers outlining the changes to the platform, researchers will also be restricted from building public apps and sharing tools with external colleagues until that manual checking system is fully up and running. Researchers were also warned that they will not be able to refresh or dispense data, only work with pre-existing data. They were also told to expect automatic logout out after 15 minutes of inactivity, with 2FA required upon re-authentication. Other technical changes include no longer being able to SSH into jobs, interactive tools being run via "isolated browsing" which restricts data transfer between web apps and the user's local system, and some restrictions on CLI use. UKB is working toward a day when the researchers using its platform store no data on their own computers, working only with that which is uploaded to the repos it hosts. However, in uploading this data to online repos, de-identified data is accidentally included in the code. UKB says it runs daily automated scans of these repos to catch errors, and provides training to researchers to help prevent these occurrences. Between old betrayals, grief, revenge and the fight for control, the problems they faced in Season 1 are far from over. And with new alliances forming, things could get even more complicated. Sola Sobowale returns as Stella in the official poster for VSL Media’s ‘The Covenant Part 2’, streaming on Netflix and Kava TV. Sola Sobowale returns as Stella, the family’s formidable matriarch, alongside Gideon Okeke , Uzee Usman , Bimbo Manuel , Segun Arinze , Ivie Okujaye and Tope Olowoniyan . South African actors Vuyo Dabula and Sibusiso Jill are also joining the cast, bringing new characters into a story already filled with family rivalries and dangerous loyalties. Now, for the date you’ll want to remember. The Covenant Part 2 premieres on Netflix across Africa on 6 November 2026, while viewers outside Africa will be able to watch on Kava TV. item.title: Former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger bets on Nagare Labs to vault the memory wall
item.description: History is littered with the ruins of failed memory technologies. But former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger believes an emerging memory tech developed by researchers at Georgia Tech using oxide semiconductors may be the exception to the rule. "Essentially, we’ve had no major forms of innovation in memory for three decades – SRAM, DRAM, and Flash as the only memory types in broad deployment," Gelsinger told El Reg . Nagare Labs' Z2RAM aims to change that by delivering a memory tech that's nearly as fast as SRAM at a density much closer to that of DRAM, while also being easier to manufacture than HBM or LPDDR. "Fundamentally, they are combining the best characteristics of DRAM, SRAM, and flash into a new device that is both dense like DRAM, fast like SRAM, and scalable like flash," Gelsinger said. "While HBM has many limitations (power, density, shoreline bandwidth) the combination of its density and performance is the best available today. This is exactly the value that Z2RAM brings, giving better density, speed and power." This explains why investor Playground Global, where Gelsinger became a partner last year, is helping to bankroll Nagare's development efforts. SRAM-like speed, DRAM-like density Founded by Georgia Institute of Technology professors and researchers Suman Datta and Shimeng Yu, Nagare Labs is the culmination of years of research into next-generation memory technologies like ferroelectrics and resistive RAM. The technology is being built on oxide semiconductors and is designed to be integrated directly onto compute logic using 3D hybrid bonding technologies. In this respect, Z2RAM will fill a similar role to AMD's 3D V-Cache SRAM stacking tech. If you're familiar with CPUs requiring additional L3 cache, AMD uses advanced packaging to bond a 64MB SRAM tile either above or below its CPU chiplets, effectively tripling their SRAM capacity. Z2RAM is similar in concept, but promises bit density upwards of 5x that of SRAM in its first incarnation. So if you were to look at a 64MB SRAM tile, Nagare's Z2RAM tiles would offer 320 MB of capacity in the same space, at bandwidth comparable to SRAM. While that may not sound like a lot of capacity compared to HBM-heavy accelerators like Nvidia's Rubin with its 288 GB capacity, or AMD's MI455X with its 432 GB, Z2RAM presents a major improvement over SRAM-based accelerators like Nvidia's Groq LPUs. Today, Nvidia's Groq 3 LPUs feature about 500 MB of SRAM per chip, necessitating thousands of accelerators in order to serve frontier LLMs at scale. Z2RAM could cut the number of chips required by 5x or more. "With the explosion of AI demand, we’ve seen an extraordinary demand in memory as AI is a memory-limited workload. With that backdrop, there is extraordinary interest and now capital available for a breakthrough that solves the bandwidth and capacity challenges that AI is creating," Gelsinger told us. item.title: Rubin telescope should find more of Earth's mysterious 'mini-moons' — including some we can study up close
item.description: null Earth almost always has more than one moon. The others are just very small, and they never stay long — but they could provide accessible and unique insights into the solar system. Temporary satellites, or mini-moons , are small asteroids that wander into Earth’s neighborhood and get captured briefly by our planet’s gravity. A typical one stays about nine months and circles Earth roughly three times before escaping back into orbit around the sun , Grigori Fedorets of Finland's University of Helsinki said in a presentation at the Europlanet Science Congress (EPSC) 2026 in The Hague in September. Fedorets' modeling suggests that the largest mini-moon around Earth at any given moment is typically only about 75 centimeters (30 inches) across. An asteroid about 3 meters (10 feet) wide should be captured every 10 to 20 years. "This is not just a theoretical construct. There is observational evidence," Fedorets said. Only two mini-moons have been confirmed to date, however — 2006 RH120 and 2020 CD3 , both discovered by the Catalina Sky Survey in Arizona. Two fireballs , seen over the Czech Republic in 2013 and Australia in 2016, were traced back to objects that had been in geocentric orbits. Two more asteroids, 2022 NX1 and 2024 PT5 , were captured only briefly, without completing a full orbit. Fedorets noted a potential third mini-moon — the recently detected Sar2901, which could also be an artificial object. Sar2901 has since faded from view but should be observable again around mid-to-late November, according to the Minor Planet Center. Small rocks, big questions Mini-moons are so small that scientists know little about them. For objects between 1 and 10 meters (3.3 to 33 feet) across, models of the near-Earth asteroid population disagree with the numbers suggested by records of fireballs in Earth's atmosphere . Mini-moons sit right in that gap, so finding more of them should show which picture is right. They may also reveal how much of the material in Earth’s neighborhood traces its origin back to our moon, as some small asteroids may be chunks of the lunar surface blasted into space by impacts. During the temporary flyby of asteroid 2024 PT5, for example, scientists found its spectrum to be closer to lunar rock than to typical asteroids, according to a 2025 study led by Theodore Kareta, which Fedorets described as the strongest evidence yet for lunar ejecta among Earth's small neighbors. Kamo’oalewa, a much larger asteroid and quasi-moon of Earth, at which China’s Tianwen-2 mission arrived in July, has been the subject of debate over possible lunar or asteroidal origins. Rubin game-changer and budget sample returns The transformative Vera C. Rubin Observatory 's 10-year Legacy Survey of Space and Time ( LSST ) should find many more mini-moons, though further work will be needed. On its own, Fedorets estimates, the survey should catch a mini-moon about once every two years. Fedorets and colleagues are setting up a dedicated system running on a v

item.title: iFixit dismantles Apple's Duo: 'You'd better baby that screen'
item.description: Apple's iPhone Duo scores higher than its foldable rivals for repairability, but don't let dust get into its delicate workings. iFixit teardown crew put a spudger and screwdriver to Apple's flagship phone and reached a provisional verdict: its repairable, up to a point, and the batteries can be replaced. The inner display and hinge, though, look daunting. The foldable inner screen is the Duo's party trick, yet reports suggest it isn't going smoothly for every owner. Some describe dead-pixel lines around the hinge, and others see horizontal lines on the right-hand side of the display. iFixit's analysis point to the Duo's clever hinge as a possible culprit, rather than a straightforward broken cable. "The damage we're seeing in photos isn't right where the display cable passes through the hinge, but slightly lower, at a point where several edges meet and change how the thin display is supported as it bends," iFixit said. There's a center support bar which, the team speculates, might not be dropping far enough. The result is stress on the screen, near to where it reportedly breaks. As for how that could happen, iFixit dropped the Duo into a bag of glowing powder, and opened and closed it a few times. "The hinge," they said, "started crunching." To be clear, the Duo performed better than rival brands' foldables in terms of dust ingress, however, there was still enough in there to make the hinge crunch. Removing that flexible display to clean it isn't for the faint-hearted. The trim around the screen wasn't much trouble, and the thin film behind the Duo's seemingly creaseless appearance peeled off fairly easily. Removing the inner screen itself, though, took heat and a pick, and was far from easy. The outer screen was much easier to remove, and accessing the batteries (there are two) was relatively straightforward, we're told. The teardown team applied voltage, and the adhesive released the power packs. The cameras, logic boards, and other components were similarly simple to extract, although iFixit notes that five different screwdriver types were needed to finish the teardown. Aside from the inner display and hinge, the Duo is relatively repairable. "Replacing them takes a lot of work," iFixit noted, "and the price could put owners off repairing the phone at all." With the kind of money the Duo demands, AppleCare+ coverage looks like a sensible safeguard, especially given the trickle of screen-failure reports. "For a first attempt, Apple has done well," iFixit observed, having provisionally given the device five out of ten, its highest score yet for a foldable. Conventional phones, such as the latest Fairphone , have, however, scored far higher. "You’d better baby that screen, Duo owners," concluded iFixit, "And maybe quit carrying around that pocket sand." ®

item.title: October full 'Hunter's Moon' dazzles in spectacular photos from around the world
item.description: null The full "Hunter's Moon" wowed stargazers with a breathtaking display of natural light when it rose to dominate the autumn sky overnight on Oct. 25-26. Here are our favorite photos captured from around the world. October's full moon is often known as the Hunter's Moon because it traditionally rose around the time that hunters would take to the newly harvested fields to catch animals to prepare as food for the coming winter. Well, in 2026 the Hunter's Moon certainly succeeded in captivating the imagination and attention of photographers, who snapped the lunar disk alongside magnificent natural vistas, glowing cityscapes and ancient wonders. Read on to enjoy the most spectacular images of the Hunter's Moon. Best photos of the full "Hunter's Moon" 2026 We begin with a beautifully detailed shot of the Hunter's Moon captured by photographer Bill Trojan, who sent in a spectacular view of October's full moon close to moonrise on Oct. 25, shortly before the lunar disk reached its point of 100% illumination. October's full moon glows orange in the evening sky. (Image credit: Bill Trojan) Next feast your eyes on an atmospheric shot of the near-full moon captured by Tayfun Coskun as the lunar disk shone balefully over the skyscrapers of San Francisco on Oct. 25 ahead of moonset. Moonset over San Francisco. (Image credit: Photo by Tayfun Coskun/Anadolu via Getty Images) Coskun also captured this incredibly well-timed shot of a passenger jet as its landing gear appeared to skim the upper edge of the Hunter's Moon, while leaving contrails in its wake. A commercial jet rendezvous with the October full moon. (Image credit: Photo by Tayfun Coskun/Anadolu via Getty Images) Veteran New York photographer Gary Hershorn was also able to line up a shot of the full Hunter's Moon rising behind the iconic architecture of the Empire State Building from Hoboken, New Jersey, on that same night. The Hunter's Moon rises behind the Empire State Building in New York. (Image credit: Photo by Gary Hershorn/Getty Images) Davide Pischettola, meanwhile, captured the moon as it loomed behind the stained glass windows and towers of the Basilica of the Madonna dei Martiri in the town of Molfetta, Italy, as a river of cloud appeared to crown the lunar disk. The moon shines behind the Basilica of the Madonna dei Martiri in Molfetta, Italy (Image credit: Photo by Davide Pischettola/NurPhoto via Getty Images) Photographer Sayim Harmanci combined the ancient with the new in his composition by positioning Earth's satellite at the heart of a neon star that shines in the city of Hakkari, Türkiye. A star shines with the Hunter's Moon over Türkiye. (Image credit: Photo by Sayim Harmanci/Anadolu via Getty Images) Our next view of the Hunter's Moon was captured by Salih Zeki Fazlioglu as it gleamed red alongside the historic Galata Tower in Istanbul, Türkiye, at the mouth of the Black Sea. The moon shines with the Galata Tower in Istanbul, Türkiye. (Image credit: Photo by Salih Zeki Fazlioglu/

item.title: Britain bets big on AI to defend against the threats AI is helping create
item.description: The UK government is throwing £130 million at AI-powered cyber defenses, including plans to deploy autonomous AI agents across critical infrastructure to hunt down security flaws before attackers get there first. The money is part of a wider £600 million-plus AI spending spree announced by the Treasury ahead of this week's Budget, with ministers also promising to tackle biological threats, bankroll British AI firms, and reduce the country's dependence on foreign technology. Of the cyber funding, £60 million will go towards a new National Cyber Shield that uses agentic AI to bolster Britain's defenses. That includes a £25 million challenge fund for UK cybersecurity firms and plans for a regulatory sandbox to test autonomous security tools across critical infrastructure, government and industry. Another £70 million will establish the National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre, using AI to sniff out vulnerabilities across Britain's infrastructure and wider economy. The announcement comes just days after the PHP2Shell security scare, which saw dozens of government websites taken offline after critical flaws were discovered in the widely used scripting language. Britain's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) worked with OpenAI to coordinate disclosure of the PHP flaws and give affected vendors time to prepare fixes, after AI-assisted researchers uncovered the vulnerabilities. Whitehall has already been experimenting with AI-powered vulnerability hunting. AI minister Kanishka Narayan said last week that the technology had uncovered 500 previously unknown security flaws across significant parts of the public sector. It remains unclear how much freedom the new AI defenders will have to act without human intervention, or when they'll be deployed. Ciaran Martin, former head of the NCSC, welcomed the investment, pointing to the week's events as evidence that Britain needs to get its cyber defenses in order. "We need to padlock our systems, and harness AI for defense," he said. The Treasury is also handing another £120 million to the AI Security Institute (AISI), which tests advanced AI systems for dangerous capabilities and researches ways to keep them under control. Cybersecurity isn't the only threat keeping ministers busy. Another £165 million will fund a National AI Biosecurity Initiative, including £100 million for what the government claims will be the world's first dedicated AI Biosecurity Lab . The independent, non-profit lab will use frontier AI models to detect biological threats and accelerate the development of vaccines and treatments. OpenAI is contributing £100 million in compute and model credits, while Anthropic is offering up to £100 million in model credits, model access and technical support. Google DeepMind and British biotech firm Basecamp Research are also involved, while the remaining £65 million will go towards biosurveillance and medical countermeasures against dangerous pathogens. item.title: Euro open source specialist proposes LLM gateway to ease token bills
item.description: European open source database service provider Aiven says it has saved 80 percent of its AI token costs internally by moving to open-weight models and is building a gateway to help devs swap models in and out as required. The Finland-based company built its business on hosting and providing open-source databases as a service, and in the last couple of years has moved into machine learning. Speaking to The Register , Ville Lehto, Aiven’s VP of strategy, said that when dealing with open source AI infrastructure, it's not trivial to make something that can run across the different clouds. However, in giving its developers access to LLMs, the company wanted to manage its own token costs and control its "own destiny when it comes to AI usage." After a wave of debate around so-called token-maxxing, developers have generally become more interested in reducing their costs by using a mix of models, including cheaper Chinese alternatives to the Western frontier models, and open-weight models which come at a lower cost. Open-weight models have publicly released learned parameters, principally their weights and biases, and can be run locally or hosted at lower cost than the frontier models from OpenAI and Anthropic. Examples include the Llama Family from Meta, Qwen Family from Alibaba Cloud, China’s DeepSeek, Mistral AI’s Medium 3.5 and Devstral and, Google's Gemma. "When it comes to this token use, as we witnessed early on this year, there are a fraction of users that are absolutely heavy users, and when it comes to their spend, a lot of it could be saved by actually using open-weight models," Lehto said. He said Aiven faced a choice to either have strict token budgets or try to find a more efficient way of using tokens. Opting for the latter, it implemented an internal gateway to help developers work with open-weight models more easily, Lehto said. "We wanted to make it as frictionless as possible. We can offer our employees different open-weight models, be it Western models or the ones from Asia, and take on the frontier models. We've been focusing on the heavy users, and with them we see roughly 80 percent decline in spend." However, since the performance of open-weight and frontier models varies, it was also important to use other metrics, such as the cost per task, he said. Aiven built its gateway around the open source framework called LiteLLM , which it hosted. It added new features such as budgeting, access management, and added other open-source components. It runs the models on rented GPUs and self-hosts the models as well. Lehto said Aiven continued to use frontier models but only to help plan work. "When it comes to actually doing things, we use a lot of open-weight models. The majority of the work is actually done with open-weight, but the most critical bits of the work are planned with frontier models. That's how we see most success at the moment." item.title: 'More missions, more often': NASA is overhauling how it selects science missions
item.description: null NASA is overhauling how it selects and develops science missions, with changes intended to reduce costs, streamline competition and get missions into space faster. The new approach, called Competition Model 2.0 (CM 2.0), was announced on Oct. 21 in an open letter from Nicky Fox, associate administrator of NASA's Science Mission Directorate (SMD), to the NASA science community. The changes, directed by NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, could significantly reshape how scientists, universities, NASA centers and commercial companies vie for future missions. "We have heard you. We have listened. We know that the burden of bringing great ideas forward has been too heavy for too long," Fox stated in the letter. The new process aims to prioritize scientific merit over unduly complicated engineering and financial planning during initial evaluations, and reduce selection timelines to encourage innovation. Fox and other top NASA science officials will provide an overview of the reforms during a virtual town hall today (Oct. 26) at 2 p.m. EDT (1800 GMT). A livestream of the event will be available here , with an opportunity for the public to submit questions here . NASA currently selects many of its science missions through competitive Announcements of Opportunity (AOs), inviting scientists and research institutions to submit proposals. Under the existing two-step process, competing teams must include thorough engineering and financial details as part of their proposals before NASA selects finalists for further study. The process can take almost three years, requiring significant investments of time and resources from teams that may ultimately never get selected. CM 2.0 aims to reduce that burden by emphasizing scientific distinction during initial evaluations, allowing teams to defer much of the engineering and financial planning until later. Instead, initial proposals will focus on the scientific objectives of a mission and a preliminary plan for how to accomplish them. NASA organizes its science missions into different classes based on their size, cost and objectives, with selection procedures varying between them. These range from smaller Explorer missions to large, expensive flagships like the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). Under CM 2.0, programs including smaller Discovery planetary missions, larger New Frontiers spacecraft and Astro-Probes, a program that focuses on mid-sized astronomy missions, will retain a streamlined version of the existing two-step process, but with nearly half of the material required for initial proposals. "This means that the original 35-months timeline will be reduced to about 19.5 months, all while having a stronger, more mature mission at the time of selection," Fox wrote. Flagship missions, meanwhile, will continue following their current procedures, which were recently revised based on lessons learned from a study of best practices examining the development of JWST.
